title: Data Privacy in the Life Insurance Industry

blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain why Nigerian life insurance companies are classified as ‘Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance’ under the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023), and describe the specific obligations this classification imposes.

Describe the types of personal data processed in the life insurance context (health data, financial data, biometric data, and claims data) and explain their sensitivity classification and the heightened protection requirements for special category data under NDPA 2023.

Identify and explain the six lawful bases for processing personal data under NDPA 2023, and apply the correct lawful basis to the principal data processing activities of a Nigerian life insurer, including underwriting, claims, marketing, fraud prevention, and regulatory compliance.

Describe the data subject rights established by NDPA 2023 (access, rectification, erasure, portability, restriction, and objection) and explain the practical procedures a Nigerian life insurer must implement to respond to data subject requests within the statutory timeframe.

Explain the role, appointment requirements, independence obligations, and reporting responsibilities of the Data Protection Officer (DPO) in a licensed Nigerian insurer, and describe the consequences of DPO under-resourcing for the insurer’s NDPC compliance posture.

Describe the purpose, scope, and methodology of Data Protection Impact Assessments (DPIAs), and identify the specific life insurance processing activities that require a DPIA under the GAID 2025 framework.

Explain the cross-border data transfer rules under NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025, applying them to the specific scenarios of reinsurance data sharing, actuarial data outsourcing, and cloud storage by Nigerian life insurers.

Describe the data breach response framework required by NDPA 2023: what constitutes a personal data breach, the 72-hour notification obligation to the NDPC, the policyholder notification requirement, and the insurer’s internal incident response obligations.

Describe the implications of the NDPC’s August 2025 sector investigation for Nigerian insurance companies, identifying the specific compliance gaps the investigation revealed and the corrective actions the Commission required.
Explain the principle of Privacy by Design, and describe how it should be embedded in a Nigerian life insurer’s PAS development, digital channel deployment, and third-party data sharing arrangements.
Describe the NDPA 2023 enforcement regime: the penalty structure, the NDPC’s inspection and investigation powers, and the criminal liability provisions for directors of non-compliant organisations.

blocks.text: 32.1 Introduction: Data Privacy as a Core Compliance Obligation

blocks.h: Life insurance is a data-intensive business. From the moment a prospective policyholder completes a proposal form, the insurer begins collecting and processing sensitive personal data: health history, financial circumstances, family composition, employment details, and biometric information. Through the life of the policy, the insurer adds payment behaviour data, service interaction records, claims history, and beneficiary information. When a claim is made, the insurer processes medical records, post-mortem reports, financial evidence, and identity documents relating to the deceased and their family. Few sectors of the Nigerian economy process personal data that is as sensitive, as voluminous, or as consequential for the individuals concerned.

Before the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023), this data was managed under the Nigeria Data Protection Regulation 2019 (NDPR), a framework that was widely acknowledged as underpowered and inconsistently enforced. The NDPA 2023, assented to by the President on 12 June 2023 and fully operationalised through the General Application and Implementation Directive (GAID 2025) from September 2025, is a fundamentally different instrument. It establishes an independent Data Protection Commission (NDPC) with genuine enforcement powers; creates a comprehensive set of data subject rights; imposes mandatory breach notification within 72 hours; and classifies large-scale processors of sensitive personal data, including all licensed insurers at scale, as ‘Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance’ subject to the highest tier of compliance obligations.

For Nigerian life insurers, NDPA 2023 compliance is not merely a legal obligation. It is a direct commercial and operational risk: the penalty for a serious breach can reach 2% of annual gross revenue; NAICOM market conduct inspections now include data protection compliance checks; and the reputational damage of a publicised data breach or NDPC enforcement action in a market where policyholder trust is already fragile is potentially irreversible. This chapter provides the comprehensive data privacy reference every life insurance professional needs.

blocks.text: 32.2 The Insurer as Data Controller and Data Processor of Major Importance

rows: Term
NDPA 2023 Definition
Insurance Context
Data Subject
The identified or identifiable natural person to whom personal data relates.
Policyholders, prospective applicants, beneficiaries, claimants, and employees of the insurer.
Personal Data
Any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.
Name, NIN, BVN, date of birth, address, health history, premium payment records, claims history, beneficiary designation.
Special Category Data
Personal data revealing health, biometric, genetic, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, sexual orientation, or criminal record.
Medical underwriting data (health history, test results, clinical reports); claims medical evidence; biometric identity verification data.
Data Controller
A person or entity that determines the purposes and means of processing personal data.

The licensed insurer. When a life insurer decides to collect health data for underwriting purposes, determines what data to collect, how it is stored, and who can access it, it is acting as a Data Controller.
Data Processor
A person or entity that processes personal data on behalf of a Data Controller.
Third parties engaged by the insurer to process policyholder data: TPA (health claims management); cloud service providers; actuarial firms processing policy data; reinsurers receiving cession data.
Data Controller/Processor of Major Importance (DCPMI)

A Data Controller or Processor that: (a) processes the personal data of more than a defined number of data subjects; (b) processes special categories of personal data at scale; or (c) engages in processing likely to result in high risk to data subjects’ rights.

All licensed Nigerian life insurers above a defined premium threshold are expressly classified as DCPMIs under NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025. The consequences: mandatory DPO appointment, mandatory DPCP submission, mandatory biennial data protection audit, enhanced NDPC oversight.

blocks.title: DCPMI Classification: What It Means in Practice

blocks.h: Being classified as a Data Controller/Processor of Major Importance is not merely a designation, it triggers a specific, mandatory compliance programme:
• Appoint a Data Protection Officer (DPO), a qualified individual with direct access to the Board or ExCo.
• Submit a Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) to the NDPC annually.
• Conduct a data protection audit every two years by a NDPC-certified data protection auditor.
• Maintain a Record of Processing Activities (RoPA) documenting all personal data processing.

blocks.text: 32.3 Types of Personal Data Processed in Life Insurance

blocks.h: Life insurance operations involve a wider range of personal data types than most other sectors. Understanding the classification of each data type, and the specific legal protections that apply, is the foundation of the insurer’s data governance framework.

rows: Data Category
Examples in Life Insurance
NDPA 2023 Classification
Key Protection Requirement
Basic identity data
Name, date of birth, NIN, BVN, residential address, email, telephone number.
Personal data: standard category.
Lawful basis required; adequate security; retention period limits.
Financial data
Income declaration; bank account details; premium payment history; surrender value; policy loan balance; BVN-linked transaction patterns.
Personal data: standard category (but sensitive in practice).
Heightened security for financial data; strict access controls; not to be shared with third parties without lawful basis.
Health data
Medical history declared on proposal form; medical examination results (blood pressure, BMI, blood glucose, HIV status); clinical reports; hospital records submitted for claims; cause of death.
Special category data under NDPA 2023: requires heightened protection.
Explicit consent or another specific permitted ground required; strict access control (need-to-know only); data minimisation principle strictly applied.
Biometric data
Fingerprint data captured for digital identity verification; facial recognition data used in eKYC onboarding; voice recognition data from contact centre calls.
Special category data under NDPA 2023.
Explicit consent required; biometric data may only be processed for the specific stated purpose; must not be used to identify individuals in other contexts.
Genetic data
DNA test results submitted as evidence in paternity disputes affecting beneficiary entitlement; genetic condition disclosures in underwriting.
Special category data under NDPA 2023.
Explicit consent; strict access controls; cannot be used for underwriting discrimination beyond actuarially justified mortality assessment.
Claims data
Death certificate; post-mortem report; accident report; beneficiary identity documents; cause of death; medical history relevant to the claim.
Mixture of special category (health, cause of death) and standard personal data.
Claims data must be retained for the claims record retention period (minimum 10 years per GAID 2025); access restricted to the claims team and authorised auditors.
Communication data
WhatsApp message content; email correspondence; contact centre call recordings; chatbot interaction logs.
Personal data (and potentially special category if content reveals health information).
Call recordings and message logs must be disclosed in a data subject access request; retention period must be defined and documented.
Employee data
Staff HR records; payroll data; performance records; CIIN CPD records; background check results.
Personal data: employee category.
Employee data processing governed by employment contract and the specific GAID 2025 provisions on employee data.

blocks.text: 32.4 Lawful Bases for Processing Personal Data

blocks.h: Every processing activity involving personal data must rest on a lawful basis. Processing without a lawful basis is unlawful under NDPA 2023 and exposes the insurer to enforcement action. The six lawful bases, with their insurance applications:

rows: Lawful Basis
Definition
Insurance Application
Key Limitation
Contract Performance (s.25(1)(b))
Processing necessary to perform a contract to which the data subject is party, or to take steps at their request before entering a contract.

Processing policy data to administer an in-force life insurance contract: calculating premiums, processing claims, maintaining policy records. This is the primary lawful basis for core insurance operations.
Can only be relied on where the processing is genuinely necessary for the contract. Using contract performance as a basis for marketing communications to policyholders is incorrect.
Legal Obligation (s.25(1)(c))
Processing necessary to comply with a legal obligation to which the controller is subject.

AML/KYC identity verification and transaction monitoring (MLPPA 2022 obligation); NAICOM regulatory reporting; NDPA 2023 data breach notification; employee data processing required by employment legislation.

The legal obligation must be a Nigerian legal obligation applicable to the insurer. A foreign legal obligation (e.g., a reinsurer’s home country requirement) does not by itself constitute a legal obligation under NDPA 2023.
Vital Interests (s.25(1)(d))
Processing necessary to protect the vital interests of the data subject or another natural person.
Extremely narrow in insurance context. Could apply where a policyholder’s life is at immediate risk and sharing their medical data with emergency services is necessary.
Not applicable to routine insurance processing. Should not be used as a fallback basis.
Legitimate Interest (s.25(1)(f))
Processing necessary for the legitimate interests of the controller or a third party, provided those interests are not overridden by the data subject’s interests or rights.

Fraud prevention (processing data to detect fraudulent claims is in both the insurer’s and honest policyholders’ legitimate interest); security monitoring of the insurer’s systems; direct marketing to existing policyholders about similar products.

Requires a three-part legitimate interest assessment (LIA): identify the legitimate interest; show the processing is necessary; confirm the interest is not overridden by the data subject’s rights. Cannot be used where consent would be more appropriate.
Public Task (s.25(1)(e))
Processing necessary for the performance of a task in the public interest or the exercise of official authority.
Limited insurance application. Potentially applicable to insurers acting as agents of mandatory insurance schemes (e.g., processing data as part of mandatory group life compliance reporting).
Applicable only where the insurer is exercising a specific public function. Not a general-purpose basis.
Consent (s.25(1)(a))
The data subject has given freely, specific, informed, and unambiguous consent to the processing of their personal data for specified purposes.

Direct marketing communications to prospective customers; using health data for purposes beyond the specific underwriting assessment; sharing policyholder data with third-party commercial partners; using data for product development research beyond what the contract requires.

Consent must be: freely given (not a condition of the contract unless strictly necessary); specific (one purpose, not a general consent to all uses); informed (the purpose must be clearly explained); unambiguous (clear positive action, not pre-ticked boxes). Consent can be withdrawn at any time.

blocks.title: Special Category Data: Additional Lawful Basis Required

blocks.h: For special category data (health, biometric, genetic), the insurer must satisfy both a standard lawful basis AND one of the specific additional conditions in NDPA 2023 s.30. The most relevant insurance conditions are: (a) Explicit consent of the data subject (the most commonly relied on basis for health data collection at underwriting); (b) Processing necessary for establishing, exercising, or defending legal claims (relevant to claims disputes and contestation); (c) Processing necessary for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine or medical diagnosis (relevant to medical underwriting activities conducted under a medical examiner’s clinical authority); (d) Substantial public interest (requires specific NDPC authorisation). The practical implication: health data collected at underwriting requires explicit consent documented in the proposal form, and that consent must be specific to the underwriting purpose. Using the same consent for marketing, product research, or AI model training requires separate, additional consent.

NDPA 2023 establishes a comprehensive suite of rights for data subjects, including policyholders, beneficiaries, claimants, and prospective applicants. The insurer must have documented procedures to receive, validate, and respond to data subject requests within the statutory 30-day timeframe. Failure to respond is an enforcement trigger.

rows: Right
What It Means
Insurance Application
Insurer’s Response Obligation
Right of Access (s.26)

The data subject may request a copy of all personal data the controller holds about them, together with information about the purposes, legal bases, retention periods, and third parties it has been shared with.
A policyholder requests all data the insurer holds about them: policy records, underwriting notes, health data, premium history, claims records, communications log.

Respond within 30 days with a complete Subject Access Request (SAR) response. The insurer must provide data in a portable format. Cannot charge a fee for standard requests. PAS must be capable of generating a complete data export per individual.
Right of Rectification (s.27)
The data subject may request correction of inaccurate personal data held about them.
Policyholder notices their date of birth is incorrectly recorded in the insurer’s system; requests correction.
Respond within 30 days. Correct the data in all relevant systems (PAS, CRM, any data warehouse). Where data was shared with third parties (reinsurers, actuarial firms), notify them of the correction.
Right of Erasure (s.28)
The data subject may request deletion of their personal data in specified circumstances (consent withdrawn, processing no longer necessary, unlawful processing).
Former policyholder whose policy lapsed 15 years ago requests deletion of all their data from the insurer’s systems.

The right of erasure is qualified: the insurer may decline where processing is necessary for legal obligations (tax records, claims records required by GAID 2025 minimum retention periods) or the establishment of legal claims. The insurer must respond within 30 days and either comply, partially comply, or explain the lawful basis for retention.
Right of Portability (s.29)
The data subject may request their data in a structured, machine-readable format for transfer to another controller.
Policyholder switching insurers requests their claims history and health underwriting data in a format the new insurer’s PAS can import.

Applicable only where the lawful basis is consent or contract performance. Respond within 30 days with data in the requested format (CSV, JSON, or XML). This right is particularly relevant for the future of portable insurance data in Nigeria.
Right to Restriction (s.31)
The data subject may request that processing of their data is restricted while a dispute about accuracy or lawfulness is pending.
Policyholder disputes the accuracy of a health underwriting note and requests restriction while the dispute is resolved.
Mark the disputed data as restricted in the PAS; do not use it for any further processing until the dispute is resolved.
Right to Object (s.32)
The data subject may object to processing based on legitimate interest or public task grounds, and to direct marketing.
Policyholder objects to receiving marketing communications from the insurer.
Stop marketing communications immediately on receipt of objection. Cannot be overridden unless the insurer can demonstrate compelling legitimate grounds that override the data subject’s interests.
Right not to be subject to solely automated decisions (s.35)
Addressed in Chapter 31: data subjects have the right to human review of adverse AI-driven decisions in insurance.
AI-recommended underwriting decline; AI-flagged fraudulent claim without human review.
Ensure human review is always applied before communicating adverse decisions. Provide explanation of the decision logic on request.

blocks.h: An individual designated by a Data Controller or Processor of Major Importance to oversee and monitor compliance with data protection obligations, provide advice on data protection matters, cooperate with the NDPC, and act as the contact point for data subjects exercising their rights. The DPO must have expert knowledge of data protection law and practice. The DPO must be provided with the resources necessary to carry out their tasks and must be able to act independently, without instructions from management on the exercise of their data protection functions.

rows: Appointment requirements

Every DCPMI (including all licensed Nigerian life insurers at scale) must appoint a DPO. The DPO may be an employee or an external consultant. If an employee, the DPO role must be clearly separated from other roles that could create a conflict of interest, a DPO who is also the Head of Marketing (which generates most of the data processing compliance challenges) is not independent. The DPO’s appointment must be registered with the NDPC.
Qualifications

Expert knowledge of NDPA 2023, GAID 2025, and data protection law and practice. Professional certification is not yet mandatory under Nigerian law, but NDPC-recognised data protection certifications (CIPM, CIPP, CDPO) are the accepted professional standard.
DPO’s core functions

Monitor compliance with NDPA 2023 and internal data protection policies. Advise the insurer on data protection obligations. Advise on DPIAs and monitor their performance. Cooperate with the NDPC and act as the NDPC’s contact point. Respond to data subject requests escalated to the DPO level. Provide data protection training to staff.
Reporting line

The DPO must report directly to the Board or ExCo, not to any functional head whose activities they may need to challenge. A DPO who reports to the Chief Marketing Officer, the Head of IT, or the Head of Compliance may face undue influence on their independent functions.
Resourcing

The DPO must be adequately resourced: time, budget for tools and training, access to all data processing activities, and authority to require management to act on compliance findings. A DPO who is given the title but not the resources or authority to function independently is not a DPO; it is a liability, because it creates the appearance of compliance without the substance.
Consequences of under-resourcing

The NDPC has signalled that nominal DPO appointments (where the individual lacks the expertise, time, or authority to function effectively) will be treated as non-compliance. The insurer that appoints a junior paralegal as DPO and expects them to manage data protection compliance alongside other duties is not meeting its DCPMI obligations.

blocks.h: A process required by NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 before commencing a new processing activity likely to result in high risk to data subjects’ rights and freedoms. The DPIA assesses: the nature, scope, context, and purpose of the processing; the necessity and proportionality of the processing; the risks to data subjects; and the measures to address those risks (including safeguards, security measures, and mechanisms to ensure compliance). The DPIA is a governance tool, not merely a paperwork exercise: its purpose is to identify and mitigate risks before they materialise, not to document risks after deployment.
GAID 2025 specifies the categories of processing that require a DPIA. The following activities in a Nigerian life insurer’s operations require a DPIA:

rows: Processing Activity
Why a DPIA Is Required
Key DPIA Findings Expected
Mitigation Measures Required
AI/ML underwriting models
Large-scale automated decision-making using special category (health) data with significant effects on data subjects (acceptance, rating, decline).
Risk of discriminatory model outputs; risk of incorrect adverse decision without human review; risk of data subjects not understanding the basis for decisions.
Human review mandatory before adverse decisions; bias testing before deployment; right to explanation documented; prohibited features list enforced.
Biometric identity verification at onboarding
Processing of biometric data (fingerprint or facial recognition) for eKYC, which NDPA 2023 classes as special category data.
Risk of biometric data breach (biometric data cannot be changed if compromised); risk of function creep (biometric data used beyond stated KYC purpose).
Biometric data stored as a hash, not raw biometric image; strict purpose limitation enforced in PAS; right to use an alternative (non-biometric) verification method offered.
Large-scale health data processing for underwriting
Processing health data from tens of thousands of proposal forms and medical examination reports at scale.
Risk of inadequate access controls allowing unauthorised access to health records; risk of data being retained beyond the underwriting purpose.
Role-based access controls (underwriting team only); automatic archiving of health data to restricted-access storage after policy issuance; retention and disposal schedule enforced.
Sharing policyholder data with reinsurers
Transfer of policyholder health and financial data to reinsurers, potentially outside Nigeria.
Risk of cross-border transfer without adequate safeguards; risk of reinsurer using data beyond the reinsurance purpose.
Data transfer agreement with reinsurer; data minimisation (only data necessary for the reinsurance treaty); NDPC adequacy assessment for the reinsurer’s jurisdiction.
Digital behavioural analytics (mobile app usage)
Using policyholder app behaviour for lapse prediction or product recommendation.
Risk of data subjects not being aware that their behavioural data is being used for predictive analytics; risk of profiling affecting policyholder rights.
Clear privacy notice disclosing behavioural analytics; opt-out mechanism for analytics beyond basic service delivery; legitimate interest assessment documented.
Contact centre call recording
Recording all inbound and outbound calls, creating a large repository of voice recordings that may contain health and financial data.
Risk of recordings being accessed for purposes beyond quality monitoring; risk of insufficient retention controls.

Clear caller notification that calls are recorded; purpose limitation (quality monitoring and dispute resolution only); retention period (12 months maximum unless subject to active dispute); access controls.

blocks.h: Nigerian life insurance operations regularly involve the transfer of policyholder personal data outside Nigeria: reinsurance data (policyholder details shared with international reinsurers); actuarial outsourcing (policy data sent to actuarial firms in South Africa, the UK, or India for modelling); cloud storage (data stored on servers outside Nigeria); and banking integration (data shared with international bancassurance partner banks). The NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 impose specific requirements on all such transfers.

rows: Data localisation (primary storage)

Under GAID 2025, the primary storage of personal data of Nigerian data subjects must be on servers physically located in Nigeria. Secondary backups may be stored outside Nigeria, subject to adequate safeguards. This means a Nigerian life insurer using a cloud PAS on international servers (AWS Ireland, Azure Netherlands) without a Nigerian primary storage instance is potentially non-compliant.
Adequacy decisions

Transfers to countries that the NDPC has determined provide an adequate level of data protection may proceed without additional safeguards. The NDPC publishes its adequacy list. Most major insurance markets are not yet on the NDPC’s adequacy list, requiring an alternative transfer mechanism.
Appropriate safeguards

Where no adequacy decision exists, transfers may proceed if supported by: Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) approved by the NDPC; Binding Corporate Rules (BCRs) for intragroup transfers; or a code of conduct or certification mechanism approved by the NDPC. For most reinsurance data transfers, SCCs incorporated into the reinsurance data processing agreement are the standard mechanism.
Reinsurance data transfers

The reinsurance relationship creates a specific data transfer challenge: international reinsurers receive policyholder name, date of birth, health summary, and sum assured for each risk ceded. The reinsurance treaty (Chapter 14) must include a data processing addendum that: identifies the reinsurer as a data processor; specifies the purposes for which the data may be used (reinsurance assessment and pricing only); includes SCCs; and obliges the reinsurer to comply with NDPA 2023-equivalent standards.
Actuarial data outsourcing

Where actuarial modelling is performed by an external firm (including cross-border), the policy data extract sent to the actuarial firm is a cross-border data transfer to a data processor. The actuarial firm must have a data processing agreement in place, and the data transfer must be covered by SCCs or another approved mechanism. Anonymisation or pseudonymisation of the data extract (removing individual policyholder identity fields and retaining only actuarially relevant data) is the most practical way to reduce the data transfer compliance burden.
Cloud storage compliance pathway

Insurers using international cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud) should: prioritise deployment in the AWS Lagos, Azure South Africa North, or Google Cloud South Africa regions (all physically within Nigeria or the continent); maintain primary storage in Nigeria with international secondary backup; review cloud provider data processing agreements for NDPA 2023 compatibility; and document the legal basis for any residual international storage.

blocks.h: A breach of security leading to the accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data transmitted, stored, or otherwise processed. A personal data breach includes: a ransomware attack that encrypts the insurer’s PAS data; a member of staff emailing a policyholder’s medical records to the wrong recipient; a third-party processor suffering a breach affecting the insurer’s data; or the theft of a laptop containing unencrypted policyholder records.
The NDPA 2023 establishes a clear breach response framework with specific timelines:

blocks.title: NDPA 2023 Data Breach Response: The Four Obligations

blocks.h: OBLIGATION 1: DETECTION AND CONTAINMENT (Immediate, within hours)

On becoming aware of a potential breach, the insurer must immediately: contain the breach (revoke compromised credentials, isolate affected systems, stop unauthorised data exfiltration); preserve evidence (logs, access records); activate the incident response team (DPO, Head of IT, Head of Legal, CEO where material); and begin documenting the nature, scope, and likely impact of the breach.
OBLIGATION 2: NDPC NOTIFICATION (Within 72 hours of becoming aware)

The insurer must notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of a breach that is likely to result in a risk to data subjects’ rights and freedoms. The notification must include: the nature of the breach; categories and approximate number of data subjects affected; categories and approximate number of personal data records affected; name and contact of the DPO; likely consequences of the breach; and measures taken or proposed to address the breach. If all information is not available within 72 hours, an initial notification must still be made, with subsequent updates as information becomes available. Note: the 72-hour clock runs from when the insurer became aware, not from when the breach occurred.
OBLIGATION 3: DATA SUBJECT NOTIFICATION (Without undue delay where high risk)

Where a breach is likely to result in high risk to affected data subjects’ rights and freedoms, the insurer must also notify the affected data subjects directly (by their registered contact details) without undue delay. The notification must: clearly describe what happened; identify what data was involved; provide the DPO’s contact details; and describe the likely consequences and the measures taken. Notification to data subjects may be delayed with NDPC agreement where law enforcement investigations would be jeopardised.
OBLIGATION 4: DOCUMENTATION (Ongoing, immediately post-breach)

All breaches (including those below the notification threshold) must be documented in the insurer’s breach register: date discovered, date of NDPC notification, nature of breach, categories of data affected, remediation actions taken, and outcome. The breach register is a required document for the biennial data protection audit.

blocks.title: Breach Notification: What NOT to Do

blocks.h: • Do NOT delay notification to conduct a full internal investigation first. The 72-hour clock cannot be extended pending investigation. File an initial notification and update the NDPC as further information becomes available.

• Do NOT treat breach notification as a PR exercise. The NDPC notification is a legal obligation. The insurer’s communications team should not manage the NDPC notification; it should be managed by the DPO and Legal.

• Do NOT assume small breaches do not require notification. A breach affecting 50 policyholders’ health data may require notification depending on the sensitivity of the data affected and the risk to those individuals.

• Do NOT fail to notify because the breach was caused by a third party (reinsurer, cloud provider, TPA). The insurer as Data Controller is responsible for notifying the NDPC even where the breach occurred at a data processor. The processor is obligated to inform the insurer promptly; the insurer is then obligated to notify the NDPC.

blocks.text: 32.10 NDPC Sector Investigation (August 2025): Implications for Insurance

blocks.h: In August 2025, the NDPC conducted a sector-wide investigation into data protection compliance across the Nigerian financial services industry, including licensed insurers. The investigation (which involved both documentary review and on-site inspections at selected companies) identified material compliance gaps across the sector. The NDPC’s published findings and enforcement actions from this investigation are the most relevant regulatory intelligence available to Nigerian insurance compliance teams.

rows: Compliance Gap Identified
Frequency Across Sector
Required Corrective Action
Lessons for Life Insurers
DPO not appointed or appointment not registered with NDPC
Very common: many insurers had no formal DPO or had designated a junior staff member without formal data protection expertise.
Appoint a qualified DPO within 30 days; register the appointment with the NDPC; provide evidence of DPO’s qualifications and reporting line to ExCo.
DPO appointment is not optional and not a junior function. The NDPC verified qualifications and reporting independence, not just that a name had been provided.
No Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) submitted to NDPC
Common: many DCPMIs had not submitted their DPCP by the NDPC’s deadline.
Submit a compliant DPCP within 60 days; future annual submissions to be made by the NDPC’s published deadline each year.
The DPCP is a substantive document describing the insurer’s entire data governance programme; it is not a tick-box form. Late or superficial submissions attract enforcement action.
No Record of Processing Activities (RoPA)
Very common: insurers could not produce a documented inventory of their personal data processing activities.
Produce a complete RoPA within 90 days; maintain it as a living document updated when new processing activities are introduced.
The RoPA must cover every personal data processing activity: underwriting, claims, marketing, HR, outsourcing. It is the foundation document for DPIAs and the DPCP.
No data subject access request (DSAR) procedure
Common: insurers had no documented process for receiving, validating, and responding to data subject requests.
Implement a DSAR procedure; designate a DSAR response team; set up a DSAR intake mechanism (email address, web form); ensure PAS can produce a complete individual data export.
In the absence of a procedure, DSAR requests will be missed or inadequately responded to, triggering enforcement.
Data retention beyond documented retention periods
Common: data was routinely retained indefinitely in legacy PAS systems without any systematic deletion or disposal.
Conduct a data retention audit; implement automated retention and disposal schedules in the PAS; delete data exceeding documented retention periods within 6 months.
GAID 2025 specifies minimum retention periods (not maximums); the insurer must also define maximum retention periods and enforce them.
Inadequate lawful basis documentation
Widespread: insurers were processing health data for underwriting without documented explicit consent, and marketing to customers without an adequate lawful basis.
Document the lawful basis for every material processing activity; update proposal forms to capture explicit consent for health data processing; update marketing consent processes.
The most substantive finding: the absence of documented lawful basis for health data processing makes all underwriting data potentially unlawful.
No data processing agreements with key processors
Very common: key third parties (medical examiners, TPAs, actuarial firms, cloud providers) had no formal data processing agreements.
Execute NDPA 2023-compliant data processing agreements with all third parties processing personal data on the insurer’s behalf within 90 days.
Third-party processor risk is the insurer’s risk. A breach at an uncontracted medical examiner firm is the insurer’s NDPC notification obligation.

blocks.h: The principle that data protection is built into the design and architecture of information systems and business practices from the outset, rather than being added as an afterthought. Privacy by Design requires the insurer to consider data protection implications at the design stage of every new system, process, or product, not after deployment. NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 require Data Controllers of Major Importance to implement data protection by design and by default.
Privacy by Design principles applied to the three highest-risk data contexts in Nigerian life insurance:

rows: PAS development or upgrade

When specifying a new PAS or significant upgrade: define the minimum data fields required for each processing activity before the system is built (data minimisation by design); configure role-based access controls so that each system user can only access the data their role requires (access control by design); configure retention and disposal schedules so that data is automatically archived or deleted at the end of its retention period (retention management by design); ensure the PAS can generate a complete individual data export for DSAR responses (rights management by design); and ensure all data at rest is encrypted (security by design).
Digital channel deployment (app, portal, WhatsApp)

When designing a new digital channel: collect only the personal data strictly necessary for the channel’s function (data minimisation); privacy notices must be presented at the first point of data collection, in plain language, before data entry (informed consent by design); analytics and tracking should be off by default, with policyholders able to opt in rather than opt out (privacy by default); and the channel’s back-end integration with the PAS must enforce the same data access controls as the PAS itself.
Third-party data sharing arrangements

When designing a new data sharing arrangement (reinsurance treaty, TPA engagement, bancassurance integration): specify in the data processing agreement the specific data fields to be shared (data minimisation); define the processor’s permitted processing purposes and explicitly prohibit secondary use (purpose limitation by design); specify the data retention period applicable to the processor; and include the right to audit the processor’s data protection compliance.
Administrative penalties (s.48)

First offence breach of NDPA 2023: up to 2% of annual gross revenue or ₦10 million, whichever is higher. Repeat or more serious breach: up to 4% of annual gross revenue or ₦20 million, whichever is higher. For a Nigerian life insurer with ₦15 billion gross premium income, a first-offence breach could attract a fine of up to ₦300 million.
Criminal liability for individuals (s.49)

Officers of a company (directors, the DPO, the CEO) may be personally criminally liable where the breach resulted from their negligence or wilful action. Criminal penalties include fines and, in serious cases, imprisonment. The personal liability provision is designed to prevent companies treating data protection fines as a cost of doing business.
NDPC inspection powers (s.43)

The NDPC may conduct inspections (announced or unannounced) of any licensed insurer’s data processing operations; require production of any document or data; interview staff; and take copies of records. An insurer that obstructs an NDPC inspection commits a further offence.
Enforcement notices (s.44)

The NDPC may issue an enforcement notice requiring the insurer to take specified corrective actions within a defined timeframe. Failure to comply with an enforcement notice is a separate, additional breach.
Suspension of processing (s.45)

In serious cases (ongoing breach causing harm to data subjects), the NDPC may order the insurer to suspend all or specific data processing activities until compliance is achieved. A suspension of core insurance data processing would make the insurer operationally unable to function.
NAICOM interaction

NAICOM market conduct inspections from 2025 include data protection compliance as an inspection item. A serious NDPC finding against an insurer may trigger a NAICOM market conduct investigation. The combination of NDPC enforcement action and concurrent NAICOM supervisory escalation represents the dual regulatory risk of data protection non-compliance in the insurance sector.

blocks.text: 32.13 Advisory: Building the Insurance Data Privacy Programme

blocks.title: Advisory: The Five Priority Actions for NDPA 2023 Compliance in a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: ACTION 1: DPO APPOINTMENT. Appoint a qualified, resourced, independent DPO with direct Board access and register the appointment with the NDPC. Do not appoint a junior staff member or combine the DPO role with a conflicting functional role. The DPO’s credibility with the NDPC depends on their independence from the functions they oversee.

ACTION 2: RECORD OF PROCESSING ACTIVITIES. Build a complete RoPA covering every personal data processing activity. This is the foundation document: without it, the DPCP cannot be completed, DPIAs cannot be properly scoped, and the insurer cannot demonstrate to the NDPC what data it processes and on what basis.

ACTION 3: LAWFUL BASIS DOCUMENTATION. Review the lawful basis for every material processing activity in the RoPA. Update proposal forms and digital onboarding to capture explicit consent for health data processing. Review marketing consent processes. Document the legitimate interest assessment for fraud prevention and security monitoring.

ACTION 4: DSAR PROCESS AND PAS DATA EXPORT CAPABILITY. Implement a documented DSAR procedure; test the PAS’s ability to generate a complete individual data export; designate a DSAR response team; and publish a clear mechanism for data subjects to submit requests (dedicated email address, form on the insurer’s website).

ACTION 5: THIRD-PARTY PROCESSOR AGREEMENTS. Execute NDPA 2023-compliant data processing agreements with all processors: medical examiners, TPAs, reinsurers (data processing addendum to the treaty), actuarial firms, cloud providers, and any other party processing personal data on the insurer’s behalf. No processor should be receiving policyholder data without a signed DPA.

blocks.title: The Single Highest Data Privacy Risk for a Nigerian Life Insurer

blocks.h: Health data collected at underwriting without documented explicit consent. Every life insurance policy in a Nigerian insurer’s portfolio that was issued after the NDPA 2023’s commencement, where the proposer’s health data was collected on a proposal form that did not contain a specific, informed, explicit consent statement for health data processing, represents a potential NDPA 2023 breach for every piece of health data in that file. For an insurer with 100,000 in-force policies, the aggregate exposure is significant. The corrective action is not to void the policies; it is to update the proposal form going forward and to rely on the contract performance lawful basis for policies already in force, supplemented by a retrospective consent exercise where feasible. This is one of the most complex legacy compliance challenges the NDPA 2023 creates for the insurance sector.

The primary Nigerian data protection legislation, assented to on 12 June 2023, establishing comprehensive data subject rights, data processing obligations, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) as the enforcement authority.
The NDPC’s primary implementation directive under NDPA 2023, effective 19 September 2025, specifying compliance requirements including data localisation, retention periods, and DCPMI obligations.

A classification under NDPA 2023 for organisations that process personal data at scale or process special category data, triggering the highest tier of compliance obligations including mandatory DPO, DPCP, and biennial audit.

Personal data in sensitive categories requiring heightened protection: health data, biometric data, genetic data, racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious beliefs, sexual orientation, and criminal record data.

A mandatory appointee for DCPMIs responsible for overseeing data protection compliance, advising on processing activities, cooperating with the NDPC, and acting as the contact point for data subject rights.
The annual compliance programme document submitted by DCPMIs to the NDPC, describing the organisation’s data governance framework, processing activities, and compliance measures.
A mandatory document cataloguing every personal data processing activity: purposes, legal bases, data categories, data subjects, retention periods, security measures, and third parties.
One of the six legal grounds permitting personal data processing under NDPA 2023: consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
A specific, informed, and unambiguous positive act of agreement to processing of special category data; stricter than standard consent; required for health data collected at underwriting.
A mandatory assessment before commencing high-risk processing activities, evaluating the nature and necessity of the processing, risks to data subjects, and required mitigation measures.
A request by a data subject for a copy of all personal data held about them, together with information on processing purposes, legal bases, and third parties; must be responded to within 30 days.
A security incident leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure of, or access to personal data.
The NDPA 2023 obligation to notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach likely to result in risk to data subjects’ rights.
The principle that data protection is built into information systems and processes from the outset, not added as an afterthought; required by NDPA 2023 and GAID 2025 for DCPMIs.
NDPC-approved contractual terms providing adequate safeguards for cross-border data transfers where no adequacy decision exists.
The GAID 2025 requirement that primary storage of personal data of Nigerian data subjects be on servers physically located in Nigeria.
